1. Catalog Overview & Key Figures

This report analyzes the active population of artificial satellites in Earth orbit, based on NORAD Two-Line Element (TLE) records. The dataset contains 14,875 actively tracked payloads. The orbital environment is largely defined by massive growth in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations over the past five years.

Data Highlights:

  • Freshness: EPOCH dates reflect the most recent orbital state vectors from space surveillance networks.
  • Orbital Density: The median inclination of 53.16° indicates a strong preference for near-polar and mid-inclination orbits, heavily influenced by modern communications constellations.

2. Launch Year Trends

The pace of satellite deployments has fundamentally changed in the current decade. The chart below illustrates the dramatic acceleration in the number of active satellites launched per year. Of the current active fleet, 13,461 (90.5%) were launched in 2020 or later.

3. Major Constellation & Operator Breakdown

The orbital population is highly skewed by a single operator. SpaceX's Starlink constellation alone comprises 10,083 satellites, representing approximately 67.8% of all active satellites in orbit.

Following Starlink, OneWeb and Planet Labs (Flock) represent the next largest fleets, though an order of magnitude smaller. This concentration of ownership underscores a significant shift from state-dominated space operations to commercial mega-constellations.

4. Orbital Regime Classification

Satellites are grouped into primary orbital regimes based on their mean motion (revolutions per day) and eccentricity:

  • LEO (Low Earth Orbit): >14 rev/day
  • MEO (Medium Earth Orbit): 1.1 to 14 rev/day
  • GEO (Geosynchronous/Geostationary): ~1.0 rev/day
  • HEO (Highly Elliptical Orbit): Eccentricity > 0.20

5. Orbital Parameter Deep Dive

The relationship between Mean Motion (a proxy for altitude) and Inclination reveals distinct "shells" of orbital activity. The massive concentration of LEO satellites (right side of the plot, >14 rev/day) contrasts sharply with the precise equatorial alignment (0° inclination) of GEO satellites (~1.0 rev/day).

6. Key Takeaways & Outlook

  • Commercial Dominance: The space environment is now dictated by commercial mega-constellations. A single network (Starlink) accounts for the vast majority of active satellites, shifting the center of gravity in space policy towards a few key corporate actors.
  • The LEO Congestion: With 86.5% of satellites in LEO, the physical crowding of specific orbital shells (particularly between 500km and 600km altitude) raises urgent questions regarding space traffic management and collision avoidance.
  • Accelerating Launch Cadence: The exponential growth curve since 2020 shows no signs of plateauing. As heavy-lift, fully reusable launch vehicles enter operation, the barrier to mass deployment will lower further, suggesting the active catalog could double again within the next 3-5 years.
